newsitem.title: USA: U.S. factory orders rebound in June.
newsitem.headline: U.S. factory orders rebound in June.

text.p: Strong demand for new commercial aircraft and cars helped fuel a rebound in new orders to factories during June, the Commerce Department said on Friday.
Orders increased 1.2 percent to a seasonally adjusted $327.9 billion following a revised 0.5 percent decline in May orders that was previously reported as a 0.7 percent fall.
Shipments, order backlogs and inventories of finished goods all strengthened in June, underlining a healthy state of affairs for the industrial sector at mid-year as well as brisk expansion plans.
The June orders increase was moderately below Wall Street economists' forecasts for a 1.5 percent pickup and was concentrated in costly and long-lasting durable goods.

Orders for durable products that are designed to last three years or more, like cars, appliances and production machinery, jumped a revised 2.4 percent to $180.7 billion instead of the 2.3 percent increase the department reported last week.
Department officials said it was the strongest monthly increase in durable goods orders since a 3.4 percent jump in January.
But orders for nondurables, like food and paper products, dropped for a second straight month, down 0.3 percent to $147.1 billion in June following a 0.6 percent decline in May.
The June factory orders report showed orders for transportation equipment climbed strongly by 7.9 percent to $42.5 billion after a 0.7 percent decrease in May.
Shipments of motor vehicles and parts gained 3.1 percent to $28.7 billion in June after a 4 percent May drop. In the automobile industry, shipments correspond to orders.
Excluding transportation, factory orders were up only 0.3 percent in June after falling in May by 0.4 percent.
Shipments of manufactured goods, which reflect more immediate demand than orders, increased 0.9 percent in June to $326.4 billion after a 1 percent fall in May.
Defence contractors' orders, which are subject to wide monthly swings, shot up by 13.4 percent to $6.26 billion in June after an 11.9 percent decrease in May.
Orders for non-defence capital goods, a measure of business' expansion plans, gained 5.4 percent to $46.6 billion in June after 1.1 percent pickup in May.
Strong business investment in expanded operations is considered one of the underlying factors girding the long-running economic expansion since the last recession in 1990-91.
Primary metals orders rose 0.3 percent to $15.6 billion in June after a drop of 2.4 percent in May.
Orders for industrial machinery, which includes computers, declined 0.9 percent to $32.5 billion following a 3.3 percent fall in May.

Inventories of finished manufactured goods rose 0.3 percent in June to $444.8 billion after a 0.4 percent May rise. The department said it was the 11th increase in the past 12 months in stocks of finished goods, suggesting manufacturers remain confident that demand will remain relatively strong.
